why-is-my-fish-gasping-at-the-surface.title: Why Is My Fish Gasping at the Surface?
why-is-my-fish-gasping-at-the-surface.metaDescription: Fish gasping at the surface almost always means low oxygen or an ammonia/nitrite spike. Here's how to tell which, and what to do in the first 10 minutes.

faq.q: Why is my fish gasping at the surface?
faq.a: It's almost always low dissolved oxygen or a water quality problem like an ammonia or nitrite spike — test your water and increase surface agitation right away.

faq.q: Can low oxygen kill fish quickly?
faq.a: Yes — severe oxygen deprivation can be fatal within hours, so treat gasping at the surface as an emergency, not something to monitor overnight.

ich-white-spots-on-fish.title: White Spots on Fish: Is It Ich? Symptoms, Causes, and Treatment
ich-white-spots-on-fish.metaDescription: Small white spots like salt or sugar grains are the classic sign of ich. Here's how it spreads, how to treat the whole tank, and how long it takes to clear.

faq.q: Is ich contagious to other fish?
faq.a: Yes — ich spreads quickly through shared water, so treat the entire tank, not just the fish showing spots.

faq.q: How long does ich take to cure?
faq.a: Most treatments take 7-14 days to fully clear an outbreak, since the parasite's life cycle includes a stage that's resistant to medication.

cloudy-fish-tank-water.title: Cloudy Fish Tank Water: Causes and How Long It Takes to Clear
cloudy-fish-tank-water.metaDescription: White or gray cloudy tank water is usually a bacterial bloom. Here's what causes it, whether to do a water change, and how long it takes to clear on its own.

faq.q: How long does cloudy tank water take to clear?
faq.a: Most bacterial blooms clear within 3-7 days on their own once the excess waste feeding them is reduced.

faq.q: Should I do a water change for cloudy water?
faq.a: A small water change is fine, but avoid a large one — removing too much of the beneficial bacteria can prolong the cloudiness rather than fix it.

how-to-cycle-a-new-fish-tank.title: How to Cycle a New Fish Tank (Fishless Cycling, Step by Step)
how-to-cycle-a-new-fish-tank.metaDescription: Cycling a new tank means growing beneficial bacteria before adding fish. Here's the fishless cycling process step by step, and how to know when it's done.

faq.q: How long does it take to cycle a fish tank?
faq.a: A fishless cycle typically takes 4-6 weeks without a bacteria starter product, or as little as 1-2 weeks with one.

faq.q: Can I add fish before the tank is fully cycled?
faq.a: It's not recommended — fish added to an uncycled tank are exposed to ammonia and nitrite spikes that can be fatal, known as new tank syndrome.

green-aquarium-water-algae-bloom.title: Green Aquarium Water: Why It Happens and How to Clear an Algae Bloom
green-aquarium-water-algae-bloom.metaDescription: Green, pea-soup-colored water is a free-floating algae bloom caused by too much light and excess nutrients. Here's how to clear it and stop it coming back.

faq.q: How do I get rid of green water in my fish tank?
faq.a: Cut back light exposure, reduce nutrients with a water change and lighter feeding, and use an algae treatment to clear the current bloom — then keep light and feeding in check to prevent it returning.

fish-swimming-sideways-swim-bladder.title: Fish Swimming Sideways or Upside Down? Swim Bladder Disease Explained
fish-swimming-sideways-swim-bladder.metaDescription: A fish floating, sinking, or swimming sideways usually has swim bladder disorder. Here's what causes it and how fasting and diet changes usually fix it.

faq.q: Will swim bladder disorder go away on its own?
faq.a: Often yes, within a few days of fasting and dietary changes, if the cause is overfeeding or constipation rather than infection.

faq.q: Can fish recover from swim bladder disease?
faq.a: Most cases caused by diet resolve fully with fasting and fiber; if it persists more than a week, water quality or a low-grade infection may be the actual cause.

ammonia-spike-established-tank.title: Ammonia Spike in an Established Tank: Causes and Emergency Fixes
ammonia-spike-established-tank.metaDescription: An ammonia spike in an older, established tank has different causes than new tank syndrome. Here's what disrupts an established bacteria colony, and how to fix it.

faq.q: Why did ammonia spike in my established fish tank?
faq.a: It usually means the bacteria colony that normally processes waste was disrupted — by overstocking, overfeeding, decaying matter, or filter media rinsed in tap water — rather than the tank never having cycled in the first place.

fin-rot-in-fish.title: Fin Rot in Fish: How to Spot It Early and Treat It at Home
fin-rot-in-fish.metaDescription: Ragged or disappearing fin edges usually mean fin rot. Here's what causes it, how to treat it, and whether fins actually grow back.

faq.q: Will fin rot fins grow back?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases — once the infection is treated and water quality is stable, fins regrow over several weeks, though the edge may look slightly different than before.

faq.q: Can fin rot kill a fish?
faq.a: Left untreated, it can progress to the fish's body and become fatal, so it's worth treating as soon as you notice ragged or receding fin edges.

why-are-aquarium-plant-leaves-turning-ye.title: Why Are Aquarium Plant Leaves Turning Yellow?
why-are-aquarium-plant-leaves-turning-ye.metaDescription: Yellowing aquarium plant leaves usually mean a nitrogen or iron deficiency. Here's how to tell if it's normal leaf turnover or an actual deficiency, and how to fix it.

faq.q: Why are my aquarium plant leaves turning yellow?
faq.a: It's usually a nitrogen or iron deficiency from irregular fertilizing — a liquid plant fertilizer on a regular schedule typically resolves it within a couple of weeks.

beginner-fish-tank-mistakes.title: 10 Beginner Fish Tank Mistakes That Kill Fish
beginner-fish-tank-mistakes.metaDescription: Most beginner aquarium problems trace back to a handful of repeat mistakes. Here are the ten most common, and the specific fix for each.

faq.q: What's the single biggest beginner fish tank mistake?
faq.a: Rushing the timeline — stocking before the tank is cycled, buying fish before researching compatibility, or treating a symptom before testing the water to find the actual cause.

why-are-my-new-aquarium-plants-melting.title: Why Are My New Aquarium Plants Melting?
why-are-my-new-aquarium-plants-melting.metaDescription: New aquarium plants often melt within days of planting. Here's how to tell normal transition melt from an actual problem, and what to do about it.

faq.q: Is it normal for new aquarium plants to lose leaves after planting?
faq.a: Yes — most plants are grown out of water at the nursery, and the leaves they grew that way can't survive underwater, so they die back while the plant regrows underwater-adapted leaves.

faq.q: How long does plant melt last?
faq.a: Typically a few days to a few weeks; new growth should start appearing within that window if the plant is otherwise healthy.

faq.q: Should I remove melting leaves?
faq.a: Yes — trim off dying leaves as they go so they don't rot and foul the water, but leave any green, healthy tissue in place.

faq.q: When should I worry it's not just melt?
faq.a: If the whole plant turns to mush, the rhizome or crown rots, or no new growth appears after several weeks, that points to rot or a light/CO2 problem rather than normal transition melt.

aquarium-plants-not-growing-light-or-co2.title: Aquarium Plants Not Growing? It's Probably Light or CO2
aquarium-plants-not-growing-light-or-co2.metaDescription: Stalled or stunted aquarium plant growth is almost always a light or CO2 limitation. Here's how to tell which one, and the fix for each.

faq.q: Why won't my aquarium plants grow?
faq.a: Slow or stalled growth is usually a light or CO2 limitation — a full-spectrum plant light run 8-10 hours a day resolves most cases, though some species need supplemental CO2 to grow well.

faq.q: How do I know if it's light or CO2 that's limiting growth?
faq.a: Start with light if you're running a basic stock fixture — it's the more common problem. If you already run a dedicated plant light for 8-10 hours a day and growth is still stalled, CO2 is the more likely bottleneck.

faq.q: Do all aquarium plants need extra light and CO2?
faq.a: No — low-light species like anubias, java fern, and java moss grow fine under a basic light with no CO2 supplementation.

holes-in-aquarium-plant-leaves.title: Holes in Aquarium Plant Leaves: What Causes It and How to Fix It
holes-in-aquarium-plant-leaves.metaDescription: Holes or see-through patches in aquarium plant leaves usually mean a potassium or micronutrient deficiency, not pests or disease. Here's how to fix it.

faq.q: What causes holes in aquarium plant leaves?
faq.a: Holes or see-through patches in otherwise healthy leaves usually point to a potassium or micronutrient deficiency, corrected with a comprehensive liquid fertilizer dosed consistently.

faq.q: Is it pests instead of a deficiency?
faq.a: Usually not — pest damage tends to be ragged, irregular bite marks on a few leaves, while a deficiency produces more uniform holes or thin patches spread across multiple leaves.

faq.q: How long until holes in leaves heal?
faq.a: The holes themselves won't heal, but new growth should come in healthy within about two weeks of consistent fertilizing.

algae-on-aquarium-plant-leaves.title: Algae on Aquarium Plant Leaves: How to Remove It and Stop It Coming Back
algae-on-aquarium-plant-leaves.metaDescription: Algae growing directly on plant leaves points to a light/nutrient imbalance. Here's how to clear it and stop it from coming back.

faq.q: How do I remove algae from aquarium plant leaves?
faq.a: Cut back light duration, treat with an algae control product, and keep plants well-fertilized so they outcompete algae for the same nutrients going forward.

faq.q: Is algae on plant leaves harmful?
faq.a: A light dusting usually isn't fatal, but a heavy coating blocks light from reaching the leaf and can smother slower-growing plants over time, so it's worth treating early.

faq.q: Why does algae keep coming back on my plants?
faq.a: Usually the light is running too long relative to the nutrients available — cutting light to 6-8 hours a day and fertilizing consistently addresses the underlying imbalance, not just the visible algae.

why-does-my-fish-tank-smell-bad.title: Why Does My Fish Tank Smell Bad?
why-does-my-fish-tank-smell-bad.metaDescription: A bad-smelling fish tank almost always means decaying organic matter or a bacterial imbalance. Here's what to check and how to fix it.

faq.q: Why does my fish tank smell bad?
faq.a: A bad smell almost always means decaying organic matter or a bacterial/ammonia imbalance — check for anything decaying in the decor, then test your water and do a partial water change.

faq.q: Will a water change fix a smelly tank?
faq.a: It helps, but only addresses the underlying cause if you also find and remove whatever's decaying — otherwise the smell tends to come back.

fish-hiding-and-not-eating.title: Fish Hiding and Not Eating? What It Means
fish-hiding-and-not-eating.metaDescription: A fish hiding and not eating is usually the earliest sign of stress or illness, before other symptoms appear. Here's what to check first.

faq.q: Why is my fish hiding and not eating?
faq.a: This is usually the earliest sign of stress or illness, before other symptoms appear — testing your water is the first step since a hidden water quality issue is the most common cause.

faq.q: How long should I wait before worrying?
faq.a: A day after a stressful event like a water change or new tankmate usually isn't a concern; several days of hiding and not eating, or other symptoms appearing, is worth acting on.

why-are-my-fish-fighting.title: Why Are My Fish Fighting? Aggression and Stocking Problems
why-are-my-fish-fighting.metaDescription: Ongoing fish aggression is usually a stocking problem, not a behavioral one. Here's how to fix tank size, species mix, and hiding spots.

faq.q: How do I stop fish from fighting?
faq.a: Add more hiding spots and visual breaks first — most aggression is territorial and eases once fish can't constantly see each other.

faq.q: Is some aggression normal in a community tank?
faq.a: Brief chasing or fin-flaring during initial introductions is common; ongoing chasing, biting, or a fish hiding constantly is not and needs addressing.

fish-died-suddenly-what-to-check.title: Fish Died Suddenly? What to Check Before Adding More
fish-died-suddenly-what-to-check.metaDescription: Occasional fish loss can happen from old age, but test your water before restocking. Here's what to check after losing a fish.

faq.q: Should I test my water after losing a fish?
faq.a: Yes, even in an established tank — a hidden water quality problem can affect the rest of your fish even if only one showed symptoms.

faq.q: How long should I wait before adding new fish?
faq.a: A few days, once you've confirmed water quality is stable and no other fish are showing delayed symptoms.

brown-tea-colored-aquarium-water.title: Brown or Tea-Colored Aquarium Water: Is It Safe?
brown-tea-colored-aquarium-water.metaDescription: Brown or tea-colored aquarium water is usually tannins from driftwood or leaves — cosmetic, not harmful. Here's how to clear it if you want to.

faq.q: Is tea-colored aquarium water safe for fish?
faq.a: Yes — tannins from driftwood or leaves are cosmetic, not harmful, and some fish species actually benefit from the slightly acidic, tannin-stained water it creates.

faq.q: How do I get rid of brown tannin water?
faq.a: Add activated carbon to your filter, or pre-soak/boil new driftwood before adding it to reduce how much it leaches.

foam-bubbles-on-aquarium-water-surface.title: Foam or Bubbles on Your Aquarium Water Surface
foam-bubbles-on-aquarium-water-surface.metaDescription: Foam or bubbles on your aquarium's surface usually mean a buildup of dissolved proteins from overfeeding or waste. Here's how to clear it.

faq.q: Why is there foam on top of my fish tank?
faq.a: It's usually a buildup of dissolved proteins from overfeeding or waste — a partial water change and more surface agitation typically clears it within a few days.

faq.q: Is foam on aquarium water harmful?
faq.a: Not directly, but it signals organic waste building up faster than it's processed, which can lead to an ammonia spike if left unaddressed.

how-to-know-if-fish-species-are-compatib.title: How to Know if Two Fish Species Are Compatible
how-to-know-if-fish-species-are-compatib.metaDescription: Fish compatibility depends on adult size, temperament, water parameters, and tank space together. Here's how to check before combining species.

faq.q: How do I know if two fish species are compatible?
faq.a: Check adult size, temperament, water parameter needs, and available tank space for each species — compatibility depends on all four together, not any single factor.
